# Agent risk and variation in manipulation tactics in Russia

\chaptermark{Electoral manipulation in Russia}


<!--[Note: in this and the Ukraine chapter, add evidence of the shift from strong opposition to society control measures. In Russia, it's the typical story: build United Russia, bring oligarchic resources under control, restrain media, and so on.] -->

During the 2011 Russian legislative election campaign, the city manager of Izhevsk, a regional capital, was filmed while speaking to a meeting of local veterans’ groups. In the video, city manager Denis Agashin speaks bluntly about the rewards the veterans can expect if they contribute to the ruling party’s victory in the polls. ‘If the party receives less than fifty percent of the vote in your district,’ Agashin declares, ‘that means nothing will change….If the party receives between 50 and 54 percent, we will fund [the local veterans’ groups] with 500,000 rubles.’ Agashin went on to add rewards for even more specific targets up to 1,000,000 rubles for a 60\% vote-share.^[See \url{http://www.newsru.com/russia/30oct2011/agashin.html} for a summary of the event, and the video clip.]  

Despite multiple efforts by opposition parties to bring political and criminal penalties against Agashin^[These included efforts to remove him from office, and pressure on the regional prosecutor to bring criminal charges. See \url{http://www.dayudm.ru/article/51302/} (Russian) for details.],  he was largely protected from punishment by the local dominance of the ruling party, United Russia’s. Others have not been so fortunate. For example, in 2009 a district court in Saratov oblast levied a 200,000 ruble fine against the chair of a precinct election commission for falsifying votes in favor of United Russia; still others have received suspended prison sentences.^[A website for the Honest Elections Public Council, a Kremlin-approved non-governmental agency, maintained a list of dozens of other incidents of arrests, administrative charges, and criminal proceedings against individuals who have allegedly helped manipulate an election. The organization and website are now defunct, but an archive is available at \url{https://web.archive.org/web/20170809084414/http://www.chest-vibor.ru/chronicles/}.]  Such punitive outcomes are not uncommon even in a relatively closed case like Russia: after the 2016 legislative election, the Russian Central Election Commission reported 32 criminal cases related to electoral manipulation, in addition to approximately 1,000 administrative cases and 300 fines [@tikhonova2016].

These anecdotes illustrate the personal risk undertaken by those who actually tamper with elections, an aspect of manipulation that has been largely overlooked by research that emphasizes the costs and risks borne by political leaders [@simpser2013;@magaloni2010;@ziblatt2009;@hyde_catch_2011]. A recent principal-agent model of electoral manipulation addresses this gap, by highlighting risks faced by agents if their patron loses the election. However, this emphasis on the risk of electoral defeat does not account for evidence that shows illegal electoral manipulation tactics are often used as substitutes, with one tactic increasing in severity as another declines [@harvey_manipulation_2016;@kuo_teorell_2017;@sjoberg_autocratic_2013]. In particular, some forms of manipulation stubbornly persist even as the risk of patron defeat increases along with growing levels of competition and democratization [@asunka2017electoral;@vanham2015sticks].  

The model presented here helps reconcile these findings by arguing electoral defeat for their patron is not the only risk that agents face. Instead, local political conditions---like active opposition parties or independent courts---can make participation in electoral manipulation costlier for agents, even if their patron remains in power, by increasing the local risks of exposure and political or criminal penalties for the perpetrator. However, agents can insulate themselves from local risks by engaging in forms of manipulation that are harder to observe and trace, such as vote-buying and voter pressure, which helps explain the persistence of these tactics even as political competitiveness increases. These hypotheses are supported by election-forensic analysis of two types of electoral manipulation, using electoral data from more than 90,000 precincts in each election year, across Russia’s eighty-plus regions during six national elections from 2003-2012. 


## Case selection: local and national political conditions in Russia

Russia provides an excellent case with which to test the theory. The country is large and diverse, with wide variation in socioeconomic variables across its 80-plus regions. There is also wide variation in local political opposition, with the ruling party’s margin of victory in the 2011 election ranging from one percentage point in the most competitive regions to 99 points in the least. National patronage consolidation has increased on average during the time period covered here, as regional power centers and oligarchic clans lost influence relative to the Kremlin. This evolution of the national political system, combined with a diversity of local political environments, provides ample opportunity to study agents’ behavior under different conditions. In addition, Russia provides a tough test for the theory. If the principal-agent dynamics proposed here can be detected in Russia, a case where patronage consolidation is relatively high and local constraints are relatively limited in the broader comparative context, principal-agent problems may be even more prevalent in less authoritarian hybrid regimes. 

Institutional reforms, organizational investments in the ruling party, strong economic growth, pressure on outside elites, and consistently high approval ratings for Putin himself strengthened the president’s position as the country’s chief patron. In the 2008 presidential election, the Kremlin successfully performed the transfer of the presidency from Putin to his chosen successor, Medvedev, while Putin took up the role of prime minister. However, as the 2011 Duma and 2012 presidential elections approached, tensions began to appear in the ‘tandem-ocracy’. Commentators began to consider Medvedev and Putin as representatives of ‘liberal’ and ‘conservative’ factions in the elite [@black2014russian]. Speculation about which of the two would run for the presidency in 2012 continued until September 2011, when Medvedev urged the United Russia party conference to endorse Putin for that office. This announcement, and its apparent disregard for the public’s role in the matter, exacerbated divisions in the elite, exemplified by the resignation of long-serving finance minister Alexei Kudrin [@butrin__2011].  In this context, United Russia won only forty-nine percent of the vote and lost more than seventy seats in the Duma---a major setback. In addition, the election prompted widespread allegations of manipulation and large protests in many Russian cities [@buranov__2011]. Since beginning his third term, Putin re-established the single-pyramid structure of patronage in Russia, after a modest fracturing during his years away from the presidency [@hale_patronal_2014, pp. 267-291].

## Building the vertical of power

As the time of writing, Vladimir Putin has been Russia's paramount leader (as either president or prime minister) for over twenty-five years; the politically tumultuous 1990s are a distant memory. However, the period was one of genuine political uncertainty and electoral risk for President Yeltsin and his allies. The multi-decade Putinite project has been, in large part, an effort to blunt those risks. The following provides a brief qualitative sketch of major events in this trajectory, illustrating the process by which the incumbent sought make it easier for other political actors to cooperate with the center, and harder to cooperate with the opposition.

The early period of economic reform in post-Soviet Russia was painful; price liberalization led to skyrocketing inflation, and the decline of the planned economy led to widespread wage arrears. Opposition to the reform agenda crystallized in Russia's holdover legislature, the Congress of People's Deputies, and its upper house the Supreme Soviet, where a mix of communist and nationalist lawmakers contended with supporters of Yeltsin's reforms. The Congress narrowly failed to impeach the president in March 1993. By September, Yeltsin (unconstitutionally) dissolved the legislature, and by October had ordered the military to seize the parliament building from parliamentarians and protesters barricaded there. 

Efforts to eliminate the threat of losing power began immediately. Afterward, parliamentary leaders were arrested, and the Ministry of Justice banned sixteen communist or nationalist organizations and eleven newspapers---including *Pravda* (though some of these bans would be lifted before the next election) [@urbanDecember1993Replication1994]. The new, 1993 constitution was developed within the presidential administration, and would enshrine what some would call 'suprepresidentialism' [@holmesSuperpresidentialismItsProblems1993]. The Central Election Commission decided to disqualify several well-known opposition parties from the December election, and ordered that party labels be excluded from ballots for the single-member district Duma deputies (thus privileging the party of power, Russia's Choice, which had a larger share of candidates with high local name recognition) [@urbanDecember1993Replication1994].

Despite increasing control over the institutional levers of power, difficult social and economic conditions produced competitive elections. In 1993, first place went to the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR), and third place to the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF), with Russia's Choice in second. The 1995 election was even worse for the Kremlin, with the opposition KPRF winning a plurality of seats: 157, compared to 55 for the party of power. The leader of the KPRF, Gennady Zyuganov, posed a significant challenge to Yeltsin in the 1996 presidential election, winning 32.5 percent of the vote to Yeltsin's 35.8 percent. Yeltsin won the second round, in part due to many Russian voters' fears of returning to the Soviet past [@mcfaulRussias1996Presidential1996], but also due to Yeltsin's deals with regional leaders and a class of newly minted oligarchs, exchanging long-term power short-term electoral support. For regional governors, the trade involved granting greater institutional independence to their regions [@paustyanTreatyRichPolitically2021]; for the oligarchs, it involved ownership of state enterprises [@treismanLoansSharesRevisited2010]. Evidence of significant electoral irregularities has been detected, especially in Russia's ethnic republics [@myagkovFraudFairytalesRussia2005].

The Yeltsin operation only became more fragile as his health declined and Russia suffered further economic disruptions. A group of some of Russia's most powerful regional elites and political exiles from Yeltsin's administration (e.g. former prime minister Yevgeny Primakov) put their resources behind a challenger party, 'Fatherland-All Russia.' The regional elites' ability to mobilize votes, along with help from supportive oligarchs, made Fatherland-All Russia a genuine threat to those in power [@hale2004origins].

The center responded to the immediate threat of Fatherland-All Russia, as well as to the longer-term challenge posed by empowered regional elites and captains of industry. The ailing Yeltsin appointed a (relatively) young Vladimir Putin as prime minister in August 1999. Putin's appointment coincided with the initiation of the Second Chechen War and a series of apartment bombings across Russia. Putin's vigorous response, especially in contrast with the unsteady president, helped raise his public profile and popularity; this, in turn, helped the pro-Kremlin Unity party narrowly defeat Fatherland-All Russia in the 1999 Duma election. On New Year's Eve 1999, Yeltsin resigned; as prime minister, Putin became acting president.

Buoyed by incumbency and his popularity, Vladimir Putin was elected president in 2000. He subsequently embarked on a years-long project of restoring power to the center. Seeing the writing on the wall, Fatherland-All Russia merged with Unity to form the ruling party United Russia. United Russia became one of the regime's primary vehicles for distributing patronage rewards [@Remington2008]. Regional governors steadily saw the wisdom in joining the party [@Reuter2010], accelerating a process by which the patronage resources of the regions were linked to the interests of the center [@Konitzer2006]. The administration utilized the law enforcement powers of the state to chasten opposition-oriented oligarchs and gain control of major television networks and major industrial enterprises [@sakwaPutinOligarchs2008]. Mikhail Khodorkovsky---once Russia's richest man, and most visible 'opposition' oriented oligarch---was arrested in 2003; following his conviction for fraud and tax evasion he was jailed until 2013. The oil company he controlled, YUKOS, was dismantled and much of its assets absorbed by state-owned companies.

Ambitious efforts in the 1990s sought to reform the Soviet-era judiciary to be more autonomous. Judges gained life tenure, and the judiciary itself a prominent role in recruiting and disciplining judges. As discussed in more detail in Chapter 6, much of these efforts were rolled back over the course of Vladimir Putin's time in office. While judges retain life tenure, at least *de jure*, the institution as a whole has become increasingly subordinated to the presidential administration over time. As a result, the Russian judicial operates in two modes: an ordinary mode where procedures are followed impartially (though with substantial prosecutorial bias), and a politicized mode when significant interests are at stake [@hendleyJudicialSystemRussia2023].

The Russian experience fits the background expectation of the theory: the incumbents facing serious threats to their power should invest heavily in the tools of social control. In this case, those tools required the subordination of regional and oligarchic patronage resources to the center, and the expansion of executive influence over the courts.

## Election manipulation in practice in Russia

Illicit manipulation of national elections in Putin-era Russia is organized in a hierarchical network, with the Presidential Administration (PA) at the top. The PA is the executive office of the president; officials who report directly to president have historically been tasked with ensuring the correct election result. Since 2016, this role has fallen to Sergey Kiriyenko, First Deputy Chief of Staff to the president [@Russias2024Election2024]. Previous architects of the system include Vladislav Surkov (deputy chief of staff 1999-2011), and Vyacheslav Volodin (2011-2016) [@kortukovSovereignDemocracyPolitics2020;@RussiasTechnocratinchiefHow]. The central administration sets targets for turnout and vote-share for the ruling party, which the regional governors are then expected to deliver.

Vote-share and turnout targets are regularly leaked and discussed in the media, perhaps as a means of creating a commitment mechanism for governors and to encourage over-production. For instance, the administration's goal for the presidential election in 2018 was 70 percent turnout and 70 percent support for Putin; while official turnout missed the target by a few points, Putin's vote-share approached 77 percent [@Russias2024Election2024]. The regions compete to out-do one another, a fact which is exacerbated by Russia's vast size. When regions in the far east post their results, regions in European Russia still have practically a full working day to meet or exceed their totals [@HePerceivesThis]. Governors who fail to meet or exceed the targets can find their careers cut short [@reuter2012subnational;@Turovskii2010;@Gorokhov2017].

With patronage rewards tied to electoral outputs, regional governors work to produce the 'correct' results using their own patronage networks and the formal structure of the state. An inadvertently leaked 2024 Putin campaign document, from the ethnic Republic of Udmurtia,  illustrates the process in detail. The 38-page document, uncovered by a journalist, lists the individuals responsible for ensuring that turnout and President Putin's vote-share meet their (lofty) targets in the region. At the top of the campaign's organizational chart is the regional governor himself. Three individuals report to the governor: his chief of staff (responsible for "organization" of the campaign), a deputy governor (responsible for "finances"), and the head of the regional election commission (responsible for coordinating the work of polling places and "party mobilization"). This structure, especially the inclusion of the chair of the election commission, highlights the merger of state resources and campaign functions [@grigoryevLeakedDocument2024]. 

Achieving the desired high-turnout scenario (80 percent) will require 932,000 votes to be cast, according to a table labeled "Mobilization plan of the campaign." Of this, the document estimates that only about 90,000 voters will turn out "organically." The disparity between the two figures indicates the herculean task facing the regional patronage network: it must deliver approximately 840,000 votes while ensuring that roughly eighty percent of them are counted for Putin. To do so, the mobilization effort reaches into practically every corner of the society. Mobilization of "Relatives SVO"---relatives of those deployed in Russia's 'special military operation' in Ukraine---is expected to yield 20,000 votes. Veterans: 25,000 votes. Residents of apartment buildings: 8,000 votes. Regional legislators are expected to turn out 35,000 votes. But the largest schemes involve workplace mobilization in industry (220,000 votes) and state-dependent sectors of the economy (69,000 votes). In these and other categories, dependent clients will be pressured not only to vote themselves, but to recruit others to vote as well. Veterans are expected to bring two additional votes (a '1+2' scheme); industrial mobilization can be 1+1 or 1+2, depending on the organization [@anonymousCampaignStrategyUdmurt2024].

While the leaked document provides granular details, the problem is not confined to Udmurtia. Across Russia, agents are tasked with mobilizing all manner of voters with some degree of dependence on the state. These include medical workers, university students, and even the parents of schoolchildren [@golosChildrenContestsThreats2018]. In some ways, Udmurtia's dependent voters got off easy; in some regions, clients have been asked to provide the personal information of as many as ten other voters that they will turn out to vote [@GolosRegionalAdministrations]. Industrial mobilization is common across the country, though it does not always boost the incumbent's vote-share [@poltoratskaiaBigBrothersMeasuring2025]. 

The document is rich with details; the authors estimate that 350 agents in the state government will oversee mobilization in the state sector (one agent to every 137 'loyalists' on average), and 1,133 agents in industrial workplaces (one per every 40 'loyalists'). It lists the major enterprises in the defense industry that will be targeted, along with large agricultural facilities. Individual turnout will be monitored through United Russia's local party secretaries, through calls to individual voters, and by representatives at the polling places. Additionally, voters who have downloaded the party's app, or click an SMS link provided by the party will have their visit to the polling place geolocated [@anonymousCampaignStrategyUdmurt2024]---a modern improvement over the old methods of having voters show special flyers to loyal election commissioners [@meduzaRussiansNotInterested2024].

Russia's hierarchical system of election administration, which is highly dependent on the executive and the ruling party, enables further manipulation. At the top, the permanent Central Election Commission oversees the work of subordinate commissions. One third of the CEC's 15 members are appointed by the President, the State Duma, and the Federation Council respectively; both houses of the legislature are dominated by United Russia and subordinate to the Kremlin. As a result, the CEC tends to be dependent on, and biased toward, the ruling party [@jarabinskyAppearancesAreDeceptive2015].

At the next level, each 'subject' of the Russian Federation (i.e. the oblasts, republics, and other regions) has its own commission. Below these are the territorial election commissions (TECs), and finally, the precinct election commissions (of which there are approximately 100,000 in a national election). Appointments to the commissions come from the level above. Subject-level commissions appoint TEC commissioners; the TECs then appoint the members of the precinct commissions within their jurisdiction and designate the chairperson. In practice, this frequently allows the regional and local administrations to staff the commissions with pliant members [@baderRolePrecinctCommissions2017]. The region-level commissioners are appointed by the regional governor and the regional legislature [@rossRegionalElectionsRussia2018]; as with the CEC, these institutions are largely subordinate to the Kremlin.

As a result of this structure, the ruling party is regularly able to install loyalists and clients as commissioners up and down the hierarchy. Precinct election commissioners can then be called on to stuff ballot boxes and forge results, to monitor pro-regime turnout, and/or to look the other way during multiple or fraudulent voting. Higher level commissions can alter the results of voting in a more wholesale manner, while also monitoring and (potentially) protecting lower-level commissioners. While some commissioners may be independent or affiliated with other parties, the most important positions for ensuring the 'correct results'---that of the commission secretary and chair---are more closely held by United Russia [@baderRolePrecinctCommissions2017].

In response to its effectiveness at publicizing illicit electoral manipulation, the independent election monitoring group Golos came under increasingly heavy legal repression after 2011. In addition to this repression, the government worked to create a parallel, state-affiliated election-monitoring structure to displace independent monitors. Golos became the first NGO targeted under Russia's 'foreign agents law,' restrictive legislation first passed after Vladimir Putin's return the presidency in 2012 [@AssociationGolosFacing]. The law initially required designated organizations to submit detailed financial accounts to the government and to label themselves as 'foreign agents' in all public-facing documents (including, for example, social media posts). For failure to comply, the original Golos NGO was fined and eventually dissolved under court order [@MoscowCourtUpholds2016]. 

A spin-off organization, designed to survive legal repression as a 'movement' (rather than an organization with legal personhood), continued to operate until 2025. The organization dissolved after its co-chair, Grigory Melkonyants, was convicted of participating in an 'undesirable organization,' a draconian designation in Russian law.^['Undesirable' organizations are foreign organizations deemed threatening to national security by the government. Designation as such requires all work related to the organization in Russia to cease; Russian banks freeze related accounts, internet service providers block related websites and third-party sites that link to banned material. Working for such an organization in any capacity can carry a years-long prison sentence [@ForeignAgentsUndesirable]. Since the law's enactment in 2015, roughly 150 foreign organizations have been so designated [@UndesirableRussia2024].] Melkonyants was sentenced to five years in prison. In its final public statement announcing its own dissolution, the organization wrote: "Unfortunately, justice does not always prevail --- one must fight for it. There is always a risk of failing. This time, that is what happened. Farewell" [@golosDissolution2025]. 



## Hypotheses

### Variation in manipulation tactic as response to agent risk

While ballot-stuffing, voter pressure, and falsification can all add to the incumbent's tally in the election, considerable scholarship has been invested in understanding why incumbents may prefer one strategy or another. Incumbents may prefer a certain mix of strategies in order to evade observation [@asunka2017electoral] and loss of legitimacy [@vanham2015sticks], due to resource constraints [@greene_why_2007] or availability [@Frye2018], to avoid appearing weak [@Harvey2020] or to evade the strictures of modern electoral procedure [@kuo_teorell_2017]. With few exceptions [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019], front-line agents' cooperation with incumbents' preferences is often assumed.

However, front-line agents do indeed have agency, and are not indifferent among the choices on the menu of manipulation. In particular, different illegal election manipulation tactics can be traced back to their individual perpetrators with varying degrees of difficulty. This affects the degree of personal risk to which the agent is exposed. Table \@ref(tab:attribution) summarizes these differences. To be clear, it is likely not typically the case that the principal is trying to get the agent to adopt one manipulation tactic, but the agent chooses another. Instead, as conditions change, it becomes harder for principals to recruit agents to perform certain kinds of tasks (e.g. precinct officials to stuff ballot boxes), forcing them to rely on different agents who perform different tasks (e.g. party operatives to buy votes).

\end{tabular}

\label{tab:attribution}

To my knowledge, there have been no prior studies of the factors that make electoral crimes more or less attributable to the perpetrator. However, there is a detailed literature in criminology that examines the 'solvability factors' that contribute to the likelihood of suspect arrest and case clearance in other crimes.^[While some research in this literature focuses on violent crime, the bulk of the literature focuses on solvability factors of non-violent 'volume crimes' like burglary.] An influential early study of policing in American cities concluded that "If information that uniquely identifies the perpetrator is not presented at the time the crime is reported, the perpetrator, by and large, will not be subsequently identified" [@greenwoodCriminalInvestigationProcess1975, p. ix]. This finding has been consistent in more recent research [@coupeModellingPoliceSuccess2001;@coupeDaylightDarknessTargeting2006;@olphinSolvingBurglaryOffences2021;@robinsonFactorsInfluencingPolice2009]. The effects can be large; one study finds that being caught at the scene increases the likelihood of attribution of a burglary or theft by as much as 20,000 percent (odds ratio 207.4); on the other hand, a simple description of the suspect increases the likelihood of attribution by only 40 percent [@robinsonFactorsInfluencingPolice2009].  

In addition, an influential approach in criminology holds that three factors must come together in space and time for a crime to occur. The third of these (in addition to motivated offenders and a suitable target) is "the absence of credible guardians against a violation" [@cohenSocialChangeCrime1979]. Guardianship can be technological, to include for example security cameras, or a ballot box that only accepts one ballot at a time. But most fundamentally, guardians "are people whose presence, proximity and absence make it harder or easier to carry out criminal acts" [@hollisCapableGuardianRoutine2013]. Election observers and un-coopted election commissioners may serve this role in the electoral context, as can sufficiently motivated ordinary citizens.

A comprehensive study of UK policing found that the strongest predictor of solvability is having caught the perpetrator at the scene of the crime, though this is rare; cases where the crime is known to have taken place in a narrow time window are also more easily solved [@UnderstandingAttritionProcess]. On the basis of these trends, criminal cases are sometimes divided into three categories [@eckSolvingCrimesInvestigation1983]. First, there are cases with so few 'leads' that no amount of police effort is likely to result in a suspect being apprehended. Second, there are cases with enough initial evidence that an arrest could be made with sufficient devotion of police effort and resources. Finally, there are those cases "where the suspect has been positively identified, [which] will usually result in an arrest, even with only minimal investigative effort" [@brandl1994relationshp].  

Electoral crimes can be mapped onto these features identified in criminology research. Falsification of the vote count is the electoral crime most easily attributable to its perpetrators. Only the election officials, who are typically publicly named individuals, can count, tabulate, and record the election results; the individuals responsible for any discrepancies are thus easily identifiable. Moreover, counting the votes takes place at a known location (the polling place), as does tabulation (higher level election commissions); these activities also take place at known times (after the close of polling). Election monitors, unsurprisingly, take advantage of these facts to detect attempted manipulations.The OSCE Election Monitoring Handbook, for instance, notes that observers "should select one of their assigned polling stations at which to observe the closing procedures, and then remain there for the entire vote count"; it goes on to list detailed descriptions of the kinds of activities that monitors should be alert to [@officefordemocraticinstitutionsandhumanrightsElectionObservationHandbook2010, p. 79]. 

Similar instructions are provided for monitoring tabulation. An election monitoring guidebook from the National Democratic Institute (NDI) states that "Monitors should take note of who is present inside the voting station.... Election officials are responsible for administering the voting process.... [monitors] should observe and record the conduct of election officials in order to deter fraud, to help correct inadvertent mistakes, as well as detect and record actual irregularities" [@nationaldemocraticinstituteHowDomesticOrganizations1995, p. 71]. Due to their power, and the fixed time and location of their efforts, election officials are obvious targets of attention for those who seek to monitor and expose election fraud. This makes committing fraud an exercise in considerable risk for such officials, if they are operating in a context where monitoring by NGOs, parties, or citizens is vigorous.
    

At the other end of the spectrum of attribution are techniques where the relevant violation happens away from the polling place, both in space and in time. The actors involved are diverse and often non-public, including voters' employers and managers [@Frye2018;@fryeWorkplacePoliticsHow2025], local mayors and councilors [@Nunez2018;@Mares2019], civic organizations [@hollandMachineClientelistBrokers2015], labor unions [@LarreguyCesarMontielOleaPabloQuerubin2017], partisan neighborhood brokers [@Szwarcberg2015;@Berenschot2019], and others. Ample scholarly evidence attests to the difficulty that even their patrons have in monitoring brokers' behavior [@Aspinall2014;@stokesBrokersVotersClientelism2013;@langstonWhyClientelistBrokers2023]. Observers likewise face difficulties. The NDI handbook notes that observers should devote some attention to the atmosphere immediately outside the polling place, and should note "the identities (*or descriptions*)" of the people involved in incidents of bribery or intimidation [@nationaldemocraticinstituteHowDomesticOrganizations1995, p. 74, emphasis added]. The OSCE handbook has detailed instructions on how to evaluate the pre-election and election-day period, but unsurprisingly makes no mention of how to observe vote-buying or voter intimidation away for the polling place [@officefordemocraticinstitutionsandhumanrightsElectionObservationHandbook2010], beyond an evaluation of the formal rules limiting abuse of government resources [@officefordemocraticinstitutionsandhumanrightsHanbookObservationElection2021]. The Carter Center takes a similar approach in its guidelines for observers [@thecartercenterElectionObligationsStandards].

Recognizing these difficulties, the Russian domestic election monitoring organization Golos aimed to recruit ordinary citizens in the observation of dispersed forms of manipulation. Training materials from Golos state: 

> "Elections are not just the voting day itself, but the three months of campaigning beforehand. During this period, voters may face pressure from their superiors and illegal campaigning. Officials who are prohibited from doing so may participate in it. You may also witness the illegal use of administrative and budgetary resources in the interests of one of the candidates. All this is called 'administrative resources.' Only the voters themselves can effectively respond to this blatantly illegal behavior."

Golos goes on to provide placards that citizens can print and distribute in public places, or post on walls, to inform others of their legal rights [@HowDealAdministrative2025]. The placard encourages citizens to record photographic, audio, or video evidence of violations, and provides QR-codes that link to the authorities' online complaint portals, and to Golos' crowdsourced election violation website. These documents all illustrate the challenges facing organizations that wish to monitor and deter election violations that take place away from the polling station, and---in the Golos example---the lengths the organization must go in order to try to make such techniques attributable and risky for perpetrators. It is perhaps not surprising in this context that Golos has been the subject of increasingly harsh legal repression, and was finally forced to disband in the summer of 2025 [@alexeystrelnikovRussiasElectionWatchdog2025].

Ballot-stuffing falls somewhere in between these two extremes. Illegal ballots can be cast by election officials, of course, but can also be cast by legitimate voters or by third-parties. However, ballot-stuffing can only occur where the ballot box is, and can only occur sometime between when voting starts and ends. As a result, it is much simpler for monitors attempt to observe this kind of manipulation than it is for vote-buying and voter-pressure, which are far more dispersed and involve a more diverse range of agents. 

Consequently, if agents are indeed motivated by the desire to avoid personal attribution of electoral misdeeds, it is to be expected that agents will be less interested in techniques higher on the ladder the more likely they are to be exposed. That is, holding other factors equal, in local areas where political opposition and activist civil society are limited, we should expect to see more falsification by election officials. As the risk of exposure increases due to greater opposition and/or civil society activity, manipulation should move down the ladder in Table \@ref(tab:attribution). Election officials should shift from falsification to ballot-stuffing, and then increasingly drop out of the manipulation enterprise in favor of less easily identifiable individuals. As the risk of exposure increases further, even these third-party individuals should be less willing to manipulate in and around the polling place; instead, the incumbent will need to rely on a broader network of agents distributed throughout society. As this dispersion increases, a given 'unit' of manipulation becomes more expensive for the incumbent, as principal-agent problems mount and monitoring agents becomes more difficult.

This insight---that election-manipulating agents constrain their principals' options---produces a unique test of the regime-strength model of manipulation. Traditionally, explanations of variation in type of electoral manipulation has emphasized political leaders and their fear of legitimacy loss [@birch2011;@Schedler2013], their ability to monitor voters' compliance [@cox1981turnout;@stokes2005], their confidence in victory [@Hauser2018] or their access to certain resources [@vanham2015sticks]. Writing in 2013, Simpser noted that "the question of why some tactics of electoral manipulation are chosen over others in particular circumstances remains an open one," but sketched an expectation that incumbents would choose more cost-effective tactics over less cost-effective ones [-@simpser2013, pp. 28-29]. 

These theories suggest distinct predictions at the national and local levels. On the one hand, in a close election, theories that hinge on legitimacy costs suggest that incumbents should prioritize fraud in less-competitive regions. This is because fraud is the most cost-effective election-day manipulation strategy, but it requires control of the local election administration in order to implement. In more competitive regions, such models would seem to predict a decline in manipulation across all strategies. The difficulty in controlling the election administration in contested regions makes fraud difficult, while vote-buying, voter pressure, and voter intimidation are all more visible strategies; being directly visible to voters, their potential legitimacy cost is high if such efforts are widespread [@Schedler2013;@birch2011]. A principal-focused theory of manipulation that emphasizes legitimacy costs should thus predict that all types of election-day manipulation will decrease with the risk of exposure, and that fraud should predominate where the risk of exposure is low.

Different predictions emerge if, instead, the cost-effectiveness of a given strategy for incumbents is in large party conditioned by *agents'* incentive structures (rather than by legitimacy costs to principals). We should expect to see fraud decrease with local risk of exposure, as in the principal-focused approach. However, we should expect to see *less attributable*, though still visible forms of manipulation, *increase* with local risk of exposure. This outcome is expected because incumbents are not deterred from manipulating by legitimacy costs; indeed, they seek to demonstrate their power and impunity through the use of manipulation [@simpser2013]. However, as local risks of exposure increase, it becomes increasingly difficult to pressure election officials into engaging in attributable falsification. Instead, incumbents must rely on less attributable techniques like vote-buying and voter-pressure, despite their significantly greater cost and lower reliability. This effect should occur even when the likelihood of severe punishment is low, since being caught up in the machinery of criminal justice has a variety of formal and informal costs that can deter participation in attributable crime [@paternosterDeterrentEffectPerceived1986]. "Official actions can set off societal reactions that may provide potential offenders with more reason to avoid conviction than the officially imposed unpleasantness of punishment" [@zimringDeterrenceLegalThreat1973, p. 174]. Among ordinary citizens contemplating tax evasion, willingness to take the risk declines as perceived risk of detection increases; an effect which is especially strong if perceived likelihood of criminal *prosecution* (not conviction) is greater than zero [@klepperTaxCompliancePerceptions1989]. This is similar to election manipulation as a non-violent crime, with individual benefits (patronage), carried out by people who are generally not career criminals. As with election manipulation, an increase in the state's ability to monitor individuals' formal income can reduce tax evasion in that sector, while incentivizing individuals to evade taxes on less-monitored income (e.g. 'moonlighting,' cash business, etc.) [@slemrodTaxComplianceEnforcement2019].

<!-- [Think about using the terms principal-risk vs. agent-risk models of manipulation? Possibly in addition to 'regime strength model of manipulation and protest'] -->

Theories of manipulation that focus solely on principals' incentives should generally favor increased election fraud. As electoral outcomes become more uncertain, both the likelihood of losing office and the likelihood of significant post-election backlash increase. Incumbents are thus in a position of needing to significantly boost their vote-count while minimizing the visibility of manipulation. Falsification (and to a lesser extent ballot-stuffing) meets these criteria most effectively. It is very cost effective, requiring only that the incumbent have influence over members of the electoral administration and that they mis-report the results of the election. It does not require large networks of agents, is easily monitored (e.g. by setting vote-share and turnout targets), and can be kept hidden from voters.  

The theory outlined in Chapter 2 produces several hypotheses that can be tested in the Russian case. First, it is expected that the incumbent regime in Russia will take steps over time to reduce principal-agent problems in the face of a genuine opposition, as we have seen above. 

Changing conditions, in turn, will influence the types of illegal electoral manipulation that we observe across the country and over time, as agents respond to risk. In particular, I expect that less attributable, more dispersed forms of electoral manipulation will be more common in regions where there is a higher risk that centralized fraud will be exposed. Since exposure carries significant risk of being caught up in the legal system, where the risk of exposure is higher, agents will become less willing to engage in attributable tactics. However, given that the incumbent controls significant patronage resources, dispersed manipulation will be used to make up for the shortfall. Specifically, I expect:

>H1: Falsification will be less common as regional political competitiveness increases.

>H2: Dispersed manipulation (e.g. vote-buying, voter pressure, and multiple voting) will increase as regional political competitiveness increases.



## Data and measures

In order to test the theory, it is necessary to estimate two types of electoral manipulation: easier-to-monitor administrative falsification and harder-to-monitor vote-buying / voter pressure. To do so, I employ two separate election forensic techniques. I use these methods to estimate the level of both types of electoral manipulation in each of Russia’s regions, per election-year. These models draw on electoral data at the precinct level (more than 90,000 precincts in each election), while second-stage models incorporate control variables at the regional (80+ regions) and election-year levels (10). In both sets of models, I include socioeconomic control variables to incorporate local context [@myagkov_forensics_2009] and reduce the risk of false positives [@deckert2013patterns].


In the original turnout-based measure of electoral manipulation developed by Myagkov et al [-@myagkov_forensics_2009], turnout by precinct in a territory is compared to a party's *absolute vote-share* across the same precincts. Precinct-level absolute vote-share is defined as the number of votes a party receives divided by the total number of eligible voters in the precinct. Increasingly large correlations between these two variables indicate increasingly suspicious results, as they show that---as turnout increases in a region---the party in question is drawing more and more voters to its side from the pool of available voters. Figure \@ref(fig:turnoutfig) provides an illustration of the method.  




```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(openxlsx)
library(lme4)
library(modelsummary)

elex_data <- read.csv(here("Russia_forensics", "Data", "analysis_data_master.csv"))
vdem_data <- read.csv(here("Russia_forensics", "Data", "vdem_final.csv"))

full_data <- elex_data %>% left_join(vdem_data, by = "year")

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(majority_minority_republic = as.factor(ifelse(republic == 1 & pct_russian_upd <= 0.51, 1, 0)))

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(ethnic_status = ifelse(republic == 1 & pct_russian_upd <= 0.51, "Majority-minority Republic",
                                                         ifelse(republic == 1 & pct_russian_upd > 0.51, "Non-minority Republic", "Oblast")))

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(electronic_vote = ifelse(year == 2021 & (master_id == 11 | master_id == 36 | master_id == 34 | master_id == 62 | master_id == 29 | master_id == 84 | master_id == 85), 1, 0))

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(age_of_regime = as.numeric(year - 2000))

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(gubernatorial_regime = as.factor(ifelse(year < 2005, "Elected",
                                                                ifelse(year > 2005 & year <= 2012, "Appointed", "Reform elected"))))


full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(jud_ind_qual_lag = as.factor(jud_ind_qual_lag))

## Adding in combined spikes file

spikes_data <- read.csv(here("Russia_forensics", "spikes_combined.csv"))
spikes_data <- spikes_data %>% rename(spikes_est = result, spikes_est_adj = result_adjusted)

full_data <- full_data %>% left_join(spikes_data, by = c("master_id", "year")) #Might double-check for dupes here

## Changing the size of GDP by pop and population variables
full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(grp_by_pop = as.numeric(grp_by_pop))
full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(grp_by_pop_small = grp_by_pop / 1000)
full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(population_small = population / 1000)

## Year as factor with 2011 as reference category
full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(year = as.factor(year))
full_data$year <- relevel(factor(full_data$year), ref = "2011")

## Violations (pre)

violations <- read.xlsx(here::here("Russia_forensics", "Data", "violations_preelex.xlsx"))
violations <- violations %>% rename(year = election_year)
violations <- violations %>% rename(complaints_pre = count)

violations <- violations %>% dplyr::select(year, master_id, complaints_pre)
full_data <- full_data %>% left_join(violations, by = c("master_id", "year")) 

#### Adjusting violations to adjust by n_precinct and for skew


full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(complaints_pre_rel = (complaints_pre / n_precincts)*100)

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(complaints_pre_rel_ihs = ifelse(is.na(complaints_pre_rel)== T, NA, asinh(complaints_pre_rel)))   # IHS of full variable (asinh(0) = 0)

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(complaints_pre_ihs = ifelse(is.na(complaints_pre)== T, NA, asinh(complaints_pre)))   # IHS of full variable (asinh(0) = 0)


## Violations (election-day)

violations <- read.xlsx(here::here("Russia_forensics", "Data", "violations.xlsx"))
violations <- violations %>% rename(year = election_year)
violations <- violations %>% rename(complaints = violations_map_count)

violations <- violations %>% dplyr::select(year, master_id, complaints)
full_data <- full_data %>% left_join(violations, by = c("master_id", "year")) 

#### Adjusting violations to adjust by n_precinct and for skew


full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(complaints_rel = (complaints / n_precincts)*100)

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(complaints_rel_ihs = ifelse(is.na(complaints_rel)== T, NA, asinh(complaints_rel)))   # IHS of full variable (asinh(0) = 0)

full_data <- full_data %>% mutate(complaints_ihs = ifelse(is.na(complaints)== T, NA, asinh(complaints)))   # IHS of full variable (asinh(0) = 0)

```


```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## Looking at absolute vote-share in 2007
library(stringi)

data2007_test <- read.csv(here("Russia_forensics", "Data", "2007.csv", "2007.csv"))
data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% mutate(region = stri_trans_general(region, "cyrillic-latin"))
data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% rename(UR = "X10.Всероссийская.политическая.партия..ЕДИНАЯ.РОССИЯ.")
data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% rename(voterlist = "Число.избирателей..внесенных.в.списки.избирателей")
data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% rename(KPRF = "X4.Политическая.партия..Коммунистическая.партия.Российской.Федерации.")
data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% rename(valid = "Число.действительных.избирательных.бюллетеней")
data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% rename(invalid = "Число.недействительных.избирательных.бюллетеней")


data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% filter(region == "Leningradskaâ oblastʹ")

data2007_test <- data2007_test %>% mutate(ur_abs_vs = UR / voterlist)

```{r turnoutfig, fig.cap="Overall turnout and absolute vote-share for United Russia (hollow circles) and the KPRF (solid circles) in Leningradskaya Oblast', 2007", echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(data2007_test, aes(x = turnout)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ur_abs_vs), shape = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = kprf_abs_vs))+
  labs(x = "Turnout", y = "Absolute vote-share") + theme_bw()

```

As the figure shows, there is a markedly different relationship between turnout and absolute vote-share for the ruling party United Russia, and the largest opposition party, the KPRF. For United Russia, higher precinct-level turnout is associated with a consistent increase in its share of the overall electorate. It is important to be clear on what absolute vote-share means. Consider the precincts in Figure \@ref(fig:turnoutfig) in which turnout approached ninety percent; in these precincts, United Russia claimed the votes of approximately seventy percent *of all eligible voters*. In relative terms, this is an even more astonishing feat. Imagine, for arithmetic ease, that such a precinct has 1,000 voters on the rolls. To win 75% of these votes with 90% turnout, United Russia would need to claim 750 out of 900 voters: an eighty-three percent relative share. 

These notional results look much different in the median precinct by turnout (where roughly 54% of eligible voters turned out). In such precincts, United Russia claimed roughly 34% of the eligible voting population. Using our hypothetical list of 1,000 eligible voters, these figures work out to 340 votes for United Russia out of 540 voters; a sixty-three percent relative vote-share. Meanwhile, absolute vote-shares for the primary opposition party have no relationship at all to turnout. Whether forty percent or ninety percent of voters are recorded as casting votes, the Communists claim roughly five percent of the voting population.

A pattern like this can be explained in two ways. First, there could be innocuous explanations. Perhaps turnout and support for the ruling is confounded by a third factor, such as income, education, urban location, or ethnicity. Perhaps, as a notional example, voters are likely to cluster in districts by education, with more educated voters both more likely to turn out *and* more likely to support United Russia. In that view, the suspicious pattern in Figure \@ref(fig:turnoutfig) could be easily explained away: the more educated on average a precinct's voters are, the more likely they are to turn out in droves (and cast their ballots for the ruling party).

The alternative explanation is electoral malfeasance. In that story, a variety of techniques are available for directly inflating the number of votes for the ruling party: e.g., fraud, coerced voting, ballot-stuffing, vote-buying, and multiple voting. Precincts vary in how susceptible they are to such techniques, for many reasons: socioeconomic characteristics, the presence or absence of observers, the skill and dedication of regime agents, and so on. The more susceptible a precinct is to such tampering, the more these techniques can be used to inflate both turnout and the ruling party's *share* of that turnout. While the approach is somewhat different, a similar logic is also used in the widely-cited method for identifying the country-level 'fingerprints' of election manipulation [@Klimek2012;@kobakStatisticalFingerprintsElectoral2016].

Distinguishing between these two stories is crucial to successful election forensics [@deckert2013patterns]. To minimize the risk of false positives---of using forensics analysis to falsely claim fraud [@eggersNoEvidenceSystematic2021]---two precautions should be taken. First, where possible, quantitative analysis should control for possible confounding variables (e.g. socioeconomic factors). Second, and more fundamentally, election forensic tools should be used in coordination with qualitative assessments of overall election integrity by experts and observers. Both approaches are taken in the subsequent analysis. The fragility of election integrity in Russia is well-documented by the domestic monitoring organization Golos, by external observers (e.g. the OSCE), and by international and local experts. I have also included region-level control variables to reduce the risk that cross-regional patterns are confounded by varying levels of income, population size, urbanity, and more across regions.

The measure developed by Myagkov et al [-@myagkov_forensics_2009] captures all forms of direct election manipulation. It does not matter for the tool whether officials stuff pre-filled ballots into the ballot boxes, brokers pay voters to show up and vote multiple times, factory workers are pressured to cast their ballots a certain way, or votes are added to the final tally at the stroke of a pen; any systematic inflation of a party's vote-share may show up in the relationship between turnout and absolute vote-share. This makes it a useful gauge of overall manipulation; it cannot, however, serve as a dependent variable in the present analysis. For the present purpose, election forensic tools must be able to discriminate between centralized techniques like falsification, and more dispersed techniques like voter pressure and ballot stuffing.

With regard to these less centralized techniques, I use a modified version of the turnout-based measure proposed by Myagkov et al [-@myagkov_forensics_2009] by comparing the share of votes cast by absentee ballot and mobile ballot-box to the ruling party’s absolute vote-share across precincts using a first-stage multilevel model [@harvey_manipulation_2016;@Moser2017]. Absentee ballots have consistently been used in Russia to facilitate vote-buying, workplace mobilization, and multiple voting [@golos_analytical_2011;@frye2014;@white2011elections], until they were phased out in 2018. Russian electoral law provides for the use of a mobile ballot box, which is---in theory---brought by election officials to voters who are homebound, hospitalized, or otherwise unable to physically visit the polling place on election day. In practice, however, the mobile ballot box also creates easy opportunities for ballot-stuffing by officials. In particular, by removing electoral officials and the ballot box from the polling place, it limits observers' ability to monitor officials' behavior.

Election reporting by the civil society group Golos provides examples of how this process can work. In one instance in the 2011 election, the Golos report notes "The chair of the [precinct electoral] commission did not announce the beginning of the mobile voting, or show the register [of mobile voters]." This violation of procedure allows election officials to stuff the mobile ballot box with whatever number of votes for the ruling party is needed. As the report continues, "Afterward, 296 people were on the list, which is too many for voting at home. All 296 people were visited in 1.5 hours" [@golos2012]. The authorities have continued to rely on such methods in subsequent elections. By 2021 (when absentee voting was no longer permissible), Golos recorded 715 procedural violations related to the mobile ballot box; this was the second-largest category of violations, accounting for 16 percent of all observed violations [@KartaNarusheniyTri2021].      

To construct an election-forensic measure of voter pressure, ballot-stuffing, and similar techniques, I replace overall turnout in the Myagkov et al model with 'nonstandard' turnout. Nonstandard, here, is shorthand for ballots cast by absentee and the mobile ballot box. The measure is generated for each of Russia's regions by comparing a party's absolute vote-share is to turnout by absentee and mobile ballot box. An increasingly large correlation between nonstandard turnout and a party's absolute vote-share indicates the party is drawing increasingly large proportions of the nonstandard vote. The steps taken to construct the measure are as follows.

Precinct-level election data was obtained from the Russian Central Election Commission for national election-years 2001, 2003, 2004, 2007, 2008, 2011, 2012, 2016, 2018, and 2021. The constitutional referendum held in 2020, which (among other things) enabled President Putin to prolong his tenure in office, is not included.^[The national referendum, the first since 1993, was excluded because of its distinctiveness as a case. While it was a political campaign, it did not involve opposing parties or candidates on the ballot. While the primary function of the constitutional reform was to 'reset' President Putin's term count to zero (allowing him to bypass constitutional term limits) the reform package was salted with 205 additional changes to the constitution to appeal to various constituencies [@teagueRussiasConstitutionalReforms2020], a prospect which complicates election-forensic interpretations of the vote. Finally, the vote itself took place during the early months of the Covid-19 pandemic, which introduced all manner of procedural changes and ad hoc administrative decisions to the administration of the vote [@hutchesonConsolidatingPutinRegime2021].] For each election year, a multilevel regression analysis was performed on the precinct-level data, using a party's absolute vote-share as the dependent variable and nonstandard turnout as the independent variable. The multilevel models incorporate random slopes and intercepts by region. The random intercepts allow for the party's baseline absolute vote-share in the absence of any non-standard votes to vary across regions. The random slopes allow the relationship between non-standard turnout and absolute vote-share to vary by region, producing the regression coefficients that are used as measures of decentralized election manipulation in the second stage.

```{r digitsuniform, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Last digits of precinct vote totals for KPRF, Moscow City 2012", out.width = '75%'}
knitr::include_graphics(here("Russia_forensics", "digits_kprf12_moscow.png"))

```


The second measure of electoral manipulation must capture falsification of results only. The digits-based test proposed by Beber and Scacco [-@beber2012] has been useful for estimating falsification of results by election officials [@weidmann_violence_2013;@sjoberg_autocratic_2013;@Cantu2014;@harvey_manipulation_2016]. Their method rests on the assumption that the ones-digit for a party's vote totals across precincts in a territory should be uniformly distributed in a clean election. That is, in the absence of human intervention, a roughly equal number of precincts should report vote totals ending in 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. Put another way, whether the number of people who turn up to vote for a particular party at a given polling place is 100, 101, 102, etc., is a highly random process, influenced by (among other things) the weather, individuals' moods and obligations, conditions on the evening commute, and so on. Figure \@ref(fig:digitsuniform) illustrates this tendency using precinct-level votes for the KPRF candidate in Moscow city in the 2012 election.

However, as Beber and Scacco demonstrate, human beings are poor random number generators; when asked to produce 'random' numbers they tend to overestimate some integers (especially zeroes and fives), and underestimate others. As a result, when precinct-level election officials are tasked with inflating a party's vote total at their precinct, they tend to over-produce certain digits. This process, when aggregated hundreds or thousands of times, can result in non-uniform distributions across the territory---a signal of human electoral falsification. Figure \@ref(fig:digitsfalse) illustrates a non-uniform distribution of digits, with significant over-representation of zeroes, for the KPRF candidate in Dagestan in the 2012 election. This type of election forensic measure captures falsification only; election results may be highly influenced by vote-buying, voter pressure, or ballot-stuffing and still generate randomly distributed last digits [@harvey_manipulation_2016]. 

```{r digitsfalse, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Last digits of precinct vote totals for KPRF, Dagestan 2012", out.width = '75%'}
knitr::include_graphics(here("Russia_forensics", "digits_kprf12_dagestan.png"))

```



I estimate centralized manipulation by formal agents (i.e. falsification of results) using three approaches. First, I follow the classic technique from Beber and Scacco, using chi-square tests for the uniform distribution of trailing digits for the ruling party and the second-place finisher in each region per election-year. I test for deviations from the uniform that are statistically significant at the .05 level for both parties; the binary variable *any fraud* is marked as 1 if either party’s results are significantly non-uniform, and 0 otherwise. This variable is used as the dependent variable in a second-stage logit model. This approach measures falsification of results only; it does not measure behaviors like stuffing the ballot box with pre-filled ballots [@Sjoberg2016].

Further research has produced more refined estimates of falsification. While relying on the same logic as Beber and Scacco [-@beber2012], Lankina and Skovoroda [@Lankina2017] propose using the deviance between the expected value for a trailing digit (10%) and its observed value, controlling for the number of precincts in a territory. I follow their measure of deviance for last-digit zero; a larger deviance indicates increasing under- or over-production of zero as a last digit, a possible signal of human tampering with results. Using the deviance measure rather than a binary indicator of significant difference from the uniform allows for a more precise test. Unlike the binary measure, which would classify a chi-squared test with a p-value of 0.049 as fraudulent but one with a p-value of 0.051 as clean, the deviance measure allows for a more continuous measure of 'fraudulent-ness.' However, the original chi-square approach has the advantage of detecting deviations in digits other than zero.

Finally, I also employ the 'resampled kernel density' method developed by Arturas Rozenas [@Rozenas2017]. The intuition behind this approach is that elections which feature human falsification may produce vote-share or turnout distributions with 'spikes'---a high number of precincts reporting certain values. These values might be numbers divisible by five due to their appeal to human beings working in a hurry (i.e. 60 percent vote-share, or 65 percent). Or they might be due to specific targets laid out by political leaders (e.g. 67 percent). However, a certain degree of 'spikiness' is to be expected for simple arithmetic reasons. To account for this, Rozenas develops an approach that estimates the percentage of precincts in 'spikes' that go beyond what would be expected. 

This approach takes the observed precinct-level results from a territory and calculates the smooth distributions of a party's vote-share and overall turnout (i.e. the distribution without any spikes or valleys). It then draws a number of samples from this distribution (i.e. a number of hypothetical elections) and computes new vote-share and turnout distributions from these samples. Finally it compares the actual distribution (with its spikes and valleys) to the sampled distributions. Where the density of precincts at a given point in the distribution (e.g. sixty percent vote-share, or seventy-five percent turnout) exceed the maximum density from the sampled distributions, those precincts are marked as potentially fraudulent. I utilized Rozenas's `spikes` package in R to estimate the percentage of fraudulent precincts in each of Russia's regions across all of the elections in the dataset.^[The package will fail to produce an estimate if the total number of votes exceeds the number of registered voters in any precinct (i.e. when turnout is greater than 100%). Since such precincts are suspicious at face value, I handle regions with any such precinct differently. In order to successfully compute the estimate from `spikes`, I first exclude any precincts with greater than 100% turnout, and then run the models. Once an estimate has been returned, I add the excluded precincts back in and compute an 'adjusted' percentage of suspicious precincts. In other words, this adjusted estimate equals the percentage of fraudulent precincts identified using Rozenas's method, plus the percentage of precincts where turnout exceeds 100 percent.] I utilize this percentage value as a dependent variable.

All three of these variables should only be sensitive to falsification. Ballot-stuffing, vote-buying, voter pressure, and other forms of electoral manipulation cannot reliably produce the deviations from expected distributions that these methods identify since they still produce random vote-shares. In the analysis below,  I model the binary *any fraud* variable using logistic regression. The deviance and 'spikes' dependent variables are modeled using OLS.

there is likely to be a core of precincts that reflect more-or-less the true level of turnout and support for United Russia in the region. Votes in these precincts are subject to less---and less direct---forms of manipulation. Like all voters in the system, they experience the effects of media bias, incumbent resource advantages, and selective access to the ballot. However, they are less subject to artificial inflation of the ruling party's vote-share through . The more the voters in a precinct are subject to the latter forms of electoral malfeasance---due to a lack of election monitors, socioeconomic conditions, or other factors---

a larger positive correlation between the share of absentee ballots and United Russia’s absolute vote-share is more indicative of these kinds of manipulation (especially after controlling for demographic factors that might affect honest use of absentee ballots).  The regression coefficient linking absentee voting and ruling-party vote-share is used as the dependent variable in a second-stage feasible generalised least squares (FGLS) regression to account for the fact that the dependent variable is itself a regression estimate [@Lewis2005].  

### Explanatory variables: local political constraint

Across all models, I operationalize local constraints in three ways in the Russian context. First, I measure *regional political opposition* by taking the United Russia's vote-share in the most recent regional legislative election and subtract it from 1. However, regional legislative election results are not available prior to the 2004 national election. In order to include data from earlier periods, I rely on the margin of victory in gubernatorial elections.^[Similarly, the results of gubernatorial elections cannot be used for all elections, since Russia abolished gubernatorial elections between 2005 and 2012.] Since there can be a mechanical difference between the two types of elections that may the value of the variable, with more parties possibly competing in the legislative election than the executive one, I first center and scale each variable according to its variance before combining them. 


This variable thus increases as United Russia's vote-share in a region decreases. A higher value for this variable indicates greater opposition contestation, reduced popularity of the incumbent, and greater opposition influence in the legislature. While these factors should directly translate into constraints on the ruling party, the measure also raises concerns about endogeneity. United Russia's vote-share in regional elections is, after all, in part attributable to electoral manipulation that it may also deploy during federal elections. I address this concern in two ways. First, as a theoretical matter, I expect that increased competitiveness will affect different types of manipulation differently, rather than being associated with generally cleaner elections. In other words, I do not argue that better showings for opposition parties will be associated with reduced manipulation---an argument that would indeed be vulnerable to accusations of reverse causation. Instead, I argue that competitiveness shifts the form that manipulation takes.

As an empirical matter, I also supplement this measure with two non-electoral measures of political competitiveness in Russia; both are based on ethnicity. Russia's administrative structure---its federal oblasts, okrugs, krais, and republics---is largely inherited from that of Soviet Russia (the Russian Soviet Federated Socialist Republic, which formed the largest constituent of the USSR). In an effort to balance their Marxist distrust of national identity with the ethnic realities they had themselves inherited from the Russian Empire, early Soviet governments built politicized ethnicity into the structure of the Union [@hajdaNationalitiesFactorSoviet2019;@smithRedNationsNationalities2013]. The need to administer a multi-ethnic, multi-lingual (and multiconfessional) state led the Soviet Union to be founded along national-identity dimensions---its constituent republics were drawn up along national lines (a titular republic for Kazakhs, for Uzbeks, for Ukrainians, etc.). The RSFSR, the largest republic, was itself subdivided into national enclaves where non-Russian ethnicities predominated. Ethnic groups that were thus recognized received privileged positions in the Soviet political structure, not least of which were organs of government for the titular territory of the national group (e.g. both a regional government for, and a communist party of, the Kazakh SSR) and party cadres recruited based on nationality [@martin2001affirmative;@slezkineUSSRCommunalApartment1994]. The Soviet Union ultimately imploded along national lines, as regional leaders took advantage of the institutional structure of the Union---its internal borders, its regional legislative bodies, its regional party structures---and nationalist movements fostered by politicized ethnicity [@sunyRevengeNationalismRevolution1993;@beissingerNationalismCollapseSoviet2009].A similarly centrifugal process took place within Russia itself, as its ethnically-defined regions likewise pushed for additional sovereignty [@kahn_parade_2000].

Subordinating these regions, with their powerful governors and extensive political machines, was a major objective of the early Putin government [@Reuter2010;@golosovGubernatorialPowersRussia2016]. As a result, those political machines assets were put to use generating electoral support for United Russia; Russia's titular ethnic republics tend to be the least politically competitive regions in the country [@hale2007correlates;@white_ethnic_2017]. Ethnic minority enclaves tend to be politically unified around United Russia, due to the coherence of their political machines, while regions with larger populations of ethnic Russians tend to allow more space for competition. I operationalize this in two ways. First, the proportion of ethnic Russians in a region is taking from the Russian Census, with interpolation between census years. Second, I categorize regions as majority-minority titular ethnic regions, non-majority titular ethnic regions, and ordinary regions (i.e. oblasts). A region is coded as majority-minority if it is both a titular ethnic homeland  and ethnic Russians make up a minority of the population (e.g. Tatarstan, Chechnya). A region is coded as  a non-minority titular ethnic region if it is formally an ethnic homeland, but ethnic Russians make up a majority of the population (e.g. Karelia). All other regions are coded as oblasts, or ordinary regions.



### Control variables

Several control variables that may influence both electoral manipulation and regional competitiveness are included in the models. In addition, some control variables must be included in order to account for potentially non-manipulative explanations for suspicious patterns in the electoral data. All socioeconomic controls are taken from the Russian Federal State Statistical Service.

Since large populations may be more difficult to control and require more resources to manipulate, I include a measure of the \textit{population size} in each region; this variable is replaced with *number of precincts* in the models of deviance. Since many retirees are directly dependent on the state for their livelihoods (and thus may be easier to pressure), but may also simply be more disposed to vote for or against the incumbent as a demographic group [@colton2003popular;@hemment_sovietstyle_2009], I include the number of \textit{pensioners} per 1,000 residents in a region. Poor individuals are likely more susceptible to vote-buying efforts and other forms of clientelism [@kitschelt2007;@stokes2013brokers], and, like pensioners, may support or oppose the government as a demographic. To address this possibility, I include a measure of the percentage of the population falling below the official poverty line, as well as each region's gross regional product per capita. Researchers have often found that rural populations are more vulnerable to electoral manipulation [@simpser_does_2012], and cities have typically been sites of greater opposition to United Russia. I thus include the percentage of a region’s population living in cities as a control. 

Several variables are measured at the election-year level. First, I include a dummy variable to control for \textit{presidential elections}, which may produce higher levels of manipulation due to their high stakes for incumbents [@simpser2013]. As I have argued in prior work, the degree to which an incumbent has consolidated control over patronage resources is a key component of their ability to manipulate elections [@harvey_manipulation_2016;@Harvey2019]. I control for the degree to which the so-called 'power vertical' has been constructed in Russia using two measures. The first measure is the nationwide share of regional governors who belong to the United Russia party, and indicator of the degree to which the Kremlin was able to consolidate control over the regional political machines [@Reuter2010,@Reuter2013].^[I collected these data myself using Russian-language Wikipedia, following linked external sources for confirmation.] The persistence of United Russia as a party of power, where previous partisan experiments by President Yeltsin and his circle failed, is largely tied to it success as a vehicle for channeling patronage resources from patrons to clients [@Remington2008,@Turovskii2010]. Lastly, I use the V-Dem measure of *subnational party control* (v2pssunpar), which measures the degree to which "a single party control[s] important policymaking bodies across subnational units (regional and local governments)." Higher values on this variable indicate greater subnational competitiveness.


## Results 


The results for the three distinct measures of falsification are presented in separate tables. Table \@ref(tab:fraudtable) reports the logit models of the *any fraud* variable, based on the Beber and Scacco digits test. Table \@ref(tab:fraudtable2) reports the results for OLS regression models of the last-digit-zero deviance indicator, and Table \@ref(tab:fraudtable3) shows results from OLS models of the resampled kernel density (RKD) indicator. All nine models tell a consistent story: for all three operationalizations of falsification, and all three measures of political openness, increased openness is associated with reduced falsification. Models 1 through 3 show this effect holds for a binary measure of falsification, which is positive if the distribution of ones-digits across precincts falls outside the uniform for any digit. They show that ordinary regions, on average, are significantly less likely than titular ethnic regions to experience falsification of this kind. The effect extends to measures of ethnicity generally, where an increasing proportion of ethnic Russians (and thus, typically, weaker political machines) yields reduced fraud. Finally, Model 3 shows that, as opposition parties perform better in the regional legislature, falsification in federal elections declines.

Models 4 and 7 show the relationship between the ethnic status of a region and the level of falsification is consistent across the deviance and RKD indicators. The baseline category for *ethnic status* in Models 1, 4, and 7 is the least competitive type of region: a majority-minority ethnic republic. The models show that Russia's ordinary regions, along with ethnic republics that lack a majority-minority population, are associated with less fraud as measured by both the deviance and RKD indicators. Similarly, Models 5 and 8 show that fraud decreases in the ethnic Russian share of the population. Lastly, the most direct indicator---regional competitiveness---is also negatively associated with both measures of falsification in Models 3 and 6. 

The effect sizes are substantively significant. The change in the level of last-digit-zero deviance between a majority-minority ethnic region and an ordinary oblast is -2.36; this represents a bigger shift than that between the first (0.13) and third (1.89) quartiles of the deviance variable. The shift is even larger when falsification is measured as the percentage of possibly fraudulent precincts using the RKD estimator. For that variable, the distance between the first and third quartiles is roughly 0.8, about a third the size of the effect for oblast' status. Effect sizes are substantially larger for the *percent ethnic Russian* variable, which also ranges from zero to one. The effect of *regional competitiveness* is smaller, but still statistically and substantively significant. A shift from the first to the third quartile in competitiveness is associated with a reduction in last-digit-zero deviance of 0.48. This is roughly the difference between the deviance value for the city of Moscow in 2004 and the Karachay-Cherkess Republic^[A majority-minority ethnic republic in the Caucasus region.] in the same year. 

Regional competitiveness shows a larger effect on the 'spikes' measure of falsification. An increase from the first to the third quartile in competitiveness reduces the estimated share of fraudulent precincts by -1.14 points, or about one-third of a standard deviation of the dependent variable. All together, the results are compelling: increasing political openness is associated with substantively significant reductions in falsificaiton operationalized in two distinct ways, across three operationalizations of political openness, and when including a suite of control variables.
